title.en: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life

text.en: Grandmother picks tiny stones out of rice before cooking. This is separation. We separate mixtures every day: tea leaves from tea, cream from milk, salt from seawater.

A mixture has two or more substances that are not chemically joined and can be separated. We separate to remove harmful or unwanted parts, to get useful parts or to get pure substances.
Handpicking removes large unwanted pieces, such as stones from rice. Winnowing separates heavier grain from lighter husk using wind. Sieving separates smaller pieces from larger ones using holes of a suitable size, like flour from bran. Magnetic separation removes iron from a mixture using a magnet.
Sedimentation lets heavier particles settle at the bottom. Decantation pours off the clear liquid on top. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The filter holds back pieces too large to pass through. The liquid and many dissolved substances can go through. Evaporation of water from salt water leaves the salt behind. This is how salt is made from seawater.
Churning curd makes tiny bits of butter gather so they can be collected. To separate sand and salt, dissolve the salt in water, filter out the sand and let the water evaporate. We often use more than one method together.

Picture loose beans and a few pebbles sitting in a tray. You can see the pebbles and lift them out one by one. Handpicking is practical when there are only a few pieces to remove.

board.text: Tray with beans and a few visible pebbles

text.en: Picture grains still attached to a cut stalk. First loosen the grains so they fall away from the stalk. Separating attached grains in this way is called threshing.
After threshing, loose grain may still be mixed with husk. Moving air carries the light husk farther than the grain. Winnowing uses the difference in how far the two materials travel.
Now watch sand fall through a sieve while larger gravel stays on top. Water is not needed here. The openings need to be larger than the sand grains and smaller than the pieces of gravel.
If the sand and gravel pieces were the same size, this sieve could let both pass or hold both back. First compare the pieces, then choose the size of the openings.
A teacher holds a magnet near a mixture of steel paper clips and dry sand. The clips follow the magnet while the sand stays in the tray. What property made that separation work?

board.text: Steel clips are attracted to a magnet

text.en: A magnet would leave bits of aluminium foil among the sand. To remove a few visible bits of foil, we can pick them out by hand. The best method depends on what the mixture contains.

board.text: Aluminium foil is not attracted like steel

text.en: Imagine a jar of water with soil stirred into it. Draw a line to mark the level of the settled soil after the jar has stood still. Before we began, many of those particles were spread through the water.

board.text: Soil settles as the jar stands still

text.en: Tilt the jar gently so the clearer water flows into another container and the settled layer stays behind. Pouring off the upper layer is decantation. Fine particles may still travel with the water.

board.text: Decantation: pour the upper layer gently

text.en: In filtration, the mixture moves through a barrier with small openings. A tea strainer catches leaves because they are too large. With a finer filter, smaller solid particles can be caught.
Try predicting what a paper filter catches when salt has dissolved in clear water. The dissolved salt can pass along with the water, so the paper will not recover it.

board.text: Dissolved salt travels through the filter
Use a different method to recover salt

text.en: Filtered pond water can still contain things our eyes cannot see. Clear-looking water from this activity is for observing, not for drinking.

board.text: Use filtered samples only for observation

text.en: Salt makers can collect seawater in broad, shallow pans. Over time, some water enters the air as water vapour. As more water leaves, solid salt crystals can form in the pan.

board.text: Water evaporates from a shallow pan

text.en: For salt, keep the crystals left in the container. If the aim is to collect the water, the water vapour would need to cool on a clean surface and condense into drops.

When curd is churned, small bits of butter join into larger clumps and can be lifted from the remaining buttermilk. A sieve for dry grain works by a different property: size before the separation begins.
Plan to recover steel clips, sand and salt from one tray. Start with the magnet while all three parts are dry. The next step is to add water so the salt dissolves while sand remains solid.

board.text: First: remove steel clips with a magnet
Next: dissolve the salt in water

text.en: Filter the remaining mixture over a container. Save the solid sand from the filter and keep the salty liquid in the container for the final step.
Keep the salty liquid in a shallow dish and allow water to evaporate slowly. This gives us a third collected material. Trace the route of each material through the steps.
Suppose two dry powders are close in size, and one dissolves in water while the other does not. Explain which property you would use first and how you would recover both powders.

board.text: Plan how to collect both solids

problem.en: How can you get salt from a mixture of salt and sand?

text.en: Add water to dissolve the salt.
Filter to remove sand, then evaporate the water to get salt.

prompt.en: Explain how a farmer separates wheat grains from husk.

requiredIdeas.en: Wind carries away the lighter husk.

commonMisconceptions.en: Forgetting that sand does not dissolve.

points.en: A mixture can be separated by physical methods.
Handpicking, winnowing, sieving and magnets work on solids.
Sedimentation, decantation and filtration work for solids in liquids.
